title: The Vanishing Crore
units_note: All money figures in ₹ lakh unless marked. Negative numbers are written in parentheses, e.g. (152).

brief.headline: Revenue up 23%. Profitable. And ₹1.4 crore of cash is gone.
brief.story: Saltwater Labs is a Mumbai sunscreen brand that sells on its own website, Amazon, Nykaa and quick-commerce apps. July to September was its best quarter ever: sales up 23%, and still profitable. But the bank balance fell from ₹1.90 Cr to ₹50L, and October's salaries and ad bills are due before month-end. The founder wants to know where the money went before calling investors.

evidence.title: Profit & loss statement
evidence.teaser: Every cost line, Q1 vs Q2

body.text: Gross margin was 70% in both quarters.
Quick-commerce sales are not driven by Meta or Google ads; they are excluded from ROAS.

evidence.teaser: Stock on hand, units and value

body.text: No expired or slow-moving SKUs flagged by the warehouse.
From 1 Aug, all quick-commerce sales (Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart across 6 cities) go through a distributor, QuikReach. Before that, Saltwater sold to Blinkit directly.

evidence.teaser: Every rupee in and out, Jul-Sep

body.text: No loans taken or repaid. No tax payments fell due this quarter. Platform fees are invoiced monthly and paid separately.
Revenue is reported net of returns and refunds.
After product cost, platform fees, logistics and channel-specific marketing.
No loan repayments, dividends or tax payments this quarter.

evidence.teaser: Who owes Saltwater money, and when it's due

rows: Blinkit direct: 30 days · QuikReach (from 1 Aug): 60 days after month-end

body.text: QuikReach has paid every invoice that has fallen due, on time. August invoices (₹63L) are due on 30 Oct. September invoices (₹90L) are due on 29 Nov.

body.text: QuikReach wants 40% more stock for September, festive season. We're the #2 sunscreen on Zepto in Mumbai now 🚀
Can we take September ads to ₹55L? CAC is creeping up but it's festive.

Why is the bank balance this low if we're profitable??

causes.label: Ad spend burned through the cash
causes.feedback: Ad efficiency did fall, and it's worth fixing. But ad spend is already inside the P&L, and the business still made ₹30L. Ads can't explain a ₹1.4 Cr cash drop.

causes.label: Inventory pile-up from the new SPF stick
causes.feedback: Units rose 42%, but stock value rose only ₹30L and days of inventory barely moved (82 → 84).

causes.label: A channel partner is paying late
causes.feedback: Almost nothing is overdue. QuikReach has paid every invoice that has fallen due, on time. The money isn't late. It isn't due yet.

causes.label: Quick-commerce sales are loss-making
causes.feedback: Quick commerce earns a 27% contribution margin, better than Amazon or Nykaa. The channel is profitable.

causes.label: Suppliers demanded advance payments
causes.feedback: Supplier dues were ₹70L at both quarter-ends, on unchanged 30-day terms. No advances were paid.

causes.label: Marketplace and platform fees jumped
causes.feedback: Fees rose ₹27L, but they're inside the P&L, and the P&L is still profitable.

causes.label: One-off capital spending
causes.feedback: Capex was ₹10L: warehouse racking and laptops.

causes.label: Returns and refunds spiked
causes.feedback: The return rate moved from 6.1% to 6.4%, and revenue is already reported net of returns.

causes.label: Growth moved to a channel that pays 60 days after month-end, so cash is stuck with customers
Website sales collapsed
causes.feedback: Website sales dipped from ₹180L to ₹170L. That's small, and that channel pays in 2 days.

causes.label: Discounting crushed margins
causes.feedback: Gross margin held at 70% in both quarters.

causes.label: Amazon held back settlements
causes.feedback: Amazon owed ₹26L in June and ₹25L in September. Nothing was held back.

causes.label: Fraud or money leaking from the account
causes.feedback: The bank statement reconciles to the rupee. Every outflow matches a cost line or capex.

causes.label: Nykaa is delaying payments
causes.feedback: Nykaa has ₹2L overdue. That's not ₹1.4 Cr.

bonus.question: October salaries and ad bills are due before QuikReach's ₹63L August payment arrives on 30 Oct. What should the founder do first?
options: Cut all ad spend until the cash recovers
Stop supplying quick commerce until the money comes in
Raise cash against the ₹1.53 Cr QuikReach receivables (invoice discounting) and negotiate shorter terms on new orders
bonus.explanation: The receivables are real money owed by a partner that pays on time. Invoice discounting at roughly 1-1.5% a month turns them into cash this week. Cutting ads or pausing quick commerce shrinks the growth that's working, and a price hike does nothing for October.

explanation.answer: Growth moved to quick commerce through a distributor, QuikReach, that pays 60 days after month-end. Every rupee sold there in August and September is still owed: ₹1.53 Cr. Receivables rose ₹1.30 Cr, which is 93% of the ₹1.40 Cr cash drop. The business didn't lose money. It lent it to its customers.
explanation.cash_bridge: ₹190L opening + ₹30L profit − ₹130L more owed by customers − ₹30L more stock − ₹10L capex = ₹50L closing.
fastest_path: Open the bank statement. Only ₹375L came in against ₹505L of sales, and quick commerce paid just ₹47L on ₹175L of sales.
Open receivables & payment terms. Quick-commerce dues went from ₹25L to ₹1.53 Cr, almost nothing is overdue, and the terms are 60 days after month-end. The cash isn't lost. It's waiting.
traps: Ad spend: ROAS fell from 3.5× to 2.3×. It's a real problem and the wrong answer, because ads are already inside a profitable P&L.
Inventory: units jumped 42%, which looks alarming, but stock value rose only ₹30L.
"A partner is paying late": the closest wrong answer. Nobody is late. The terms changed, and growth piled onto the slowest-paying channel.
explanation.lesson: Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact. Fast growth on long credit terms can sink a profitable company.
